title: Is Spark's `sort()`/`orderBy()` stable (no — Spark does not preserve the original order of rows with equal sort keys due to distributed sorting; simulate stable sort by adding a tie-breaker column like `monotonically_increasing_id`)?

s1_definition.profdef: A sort is stable when two rows that have equal sort keys keep their original relative order after sorting. Spark's `sort()` and `orderBy()` are not guaranteed to be stable, because the data is partitioned across many executors and sorted in parallel, so the final interleaving of rows with equal keys depends on partitioning, task scheduling, and merge order rather than on their original input position. To get deterministic, stable-like behavior you add an explicit tie-breaker column to the sort so no two rows are truly equal on the full sort key.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a pile of trade slips, and several slips are all for the same amount of fifty thousand rupees. You ask ten clerks (executors) to each sort their own stack by amount and then you merge the stacks. The slips for fifty thousand will all end up grouped together, but whether Rajesh's slip comes before Priya's slip among those equal-amount ones depends on which clerk had which slip and who finished first. There is no promise that they stay in the order you originally handed them out. If you want a guaranteed order, you must also sort by something unique like the slip's sequence number, so ties are broken the same way every time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spark sort is not stable because parallel sorting reorders equal keys, so add a unique tie-breaker column when you need deterministic ordering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A sort is stable when two rows that have equal sort keys keep their original relative order after sorting. Spark's `sort()` and `orderBy()` are not guaranteed to be stable, because the data is partitioned across many executors and sorted in parallel, so the final interleaving of rows with equal keys depends on partitioning, task scheduling, and merge order rather than on their original input position. To get deterministic, stable-like behavior you add an explicit tie-breaker column to the sort so no two rows are truly equal on the full sort key.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a pile of trade slips, and several slips are all for the same amount of fifty thousand rupees. You ask ten clerks (executors) to each sort their own stack by amount and then you merge the stacks. The slips for fifty thousand will all end up grouped together, but whether Rajesh's slip comes before Priya's slip among those equal-amount ones depends on which clerk had which slip and who finished first. There is no promise that they stay in the order you originally handed them out. If you want a guaranteed order, you must also sort by something unique like the slip's sequence number, so ties are broken the same way every time.

**One line to remember:** Spark sort is not stable because parallel sorting reorders equal keys, so add a unique tie-breaker column when you need deterministic ordering.

sections.s2_technical:
In a single-machine sort, like Java's `Collections.sort`, stability can be guaranteed because there is one list and one algorithm that preserves input order for equal elements. Spark is different because a DataFrame is split into partitions spread across executors. When you call `orderBy("amount")`, Spark performs a range-partitioning shuffle so that all rows in a given amount range land on the same partition, then sorts each partition locally. The rows with equal amounts can come from several original partitions, arrive in an order determined by the shuffle, and be merged in a way that does not reflect their original positions. So two runs of the same job can place equal-key rows in different relative orders, especially if the input itself was produced in parallel.

This matters whenever downstream logic assumes a specific order among ties. For example if you sort trades by amount and then take the first row per amount expecting "the earliest submitted", you can silently get a different row on each run. The fix is to make the sort key unique by adding a tie-breaker. If your data has a natural monotonic column like a trade timestamp plus a sequence number, sort by `orderBy("amount", "trade_seq")`. If there is no such column, Spark provides `monotonically_increasing_id()`, which generates increasing but not necessarily consecutive long values; you add it as a column and include it in the sort: `df.withColumn("rid", monotonically_increasing_id()).orderBy("amount", "rid")`. Now every row has a unique full sort key, so the order is deterministic.

A senior-level nuance is that `monotonically_increasing_id()` reflects the current partitioning at the moment it is assigned, not the original source order, so it gives you determinism and repeatability but not necessarily "insertion order" unless you capture the id right after reading in a known order. For true source order you capture the id at read time or use `input_file_name()` plus a row index. Another nuance is that window functions like `row_number() over (partition by ... order by ...)` suffer the same tie problem, so you must put a unique column in the window's order by to get reproducible numbering. The practical banking rule is simple: never rely on the order of equal keys from a bare sort; always add a deterministic tie-breaker when correctness or reproducibility depends on it, such as picking a single representative row, generating sequence numbers, or producing audit-stable output files.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the settlement team sorts the day's trades by amount to produce a ranked report, and a downstream step picks the top row for each amount bucket as the "representative" trade for reconciliation. On Monday the representative for the fifty-thousand bucket was Rajesh's trade; on Tuesday, with identical data, it was Priya's. Nothing in the business changed. The cause is exactly the unstable-sort behavior: among equal amounts, the parallel sort put a different row first each run.

This is exactly how Spark's non-stable sort behaves. Equal keys have no guaranteed relative order because they are sorted across partitions in parallel and merged non-deterministically, so "the first row for this amount" is not stable between runs.

Problem 2 — The team needs a deterministic, reproducible report so auditors see the same ordering every time. The fix is to add a tie-breaker that makes every row's sort key unique, either a natural sequence column or a generated monotonically increasing id, and include it in the order by.

Because spinning up a real cluster is heavy, this runnable demo simulates distributed sorting in plain Java. A `Partitioner` splits trades into several partitions to mimic executors. A `ParallelSorter` sorts each partition locally and merges them in an order that can vary, reproducing the instability. A `StableSorter` adds a tie-breaker, either a natural sequence number or a generated monotonic id, and includes it so the result is deterministic. The demo sorts the same trades twice with the unstable approach to show the representative row changes, then twice with the stable approach to show it stays identical.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five trades, three of which share the amount fifty thousand (TRD-1, TRD-2, TRD-3), plus one at thirty thousand and one at seventy thousand, each with a natural trade sequence number.

Step 1: For the unstable path run one, the partitioner splits the five trades across four buckets using seed zero, so a particular arrangement of rows lands in each bucket. Each bucket is sorted by amount only. The buckets are concatenated and sorted by amount only, which groups the three fifty-thousand trades together but in an order that reflects the bucket arrangement, not the original sequence.

Step 2: The code picks the first fifty-thousand trade as the representative for run one, which happens to be one specific trade id.

Step 3: For the unstable path run two, the partitioner uses seed two, so rows land in different buckets. The same amount-only sort groups the fifty-thousand trades again but in a different relative order, and the representative picked is a different trade id. The log shows the two runs disagree, proving instability.

Step 4: For the stable path run one, the partitioner uses seed zero again, but now the sorter orders by amount and then by the unique trade sequence number. Among the fifty-thousand trades, TRD-1 with sequence one comes first.

Step 5: For the stable path run two with seed two, even though partitioning differs, the full sort key amount-then-sequence is unique, so TRD-1 is again first. The log shows both runs agree, proving determinism.

Final output:

```
Oct 30, 2026 7:09:02 AM com.bank.sort.ParallelSorter sortByAmount
WARNING: Parallel sort done (NO tie-breaker) — order of equal amounts is NOT guaranteed
WARNING: UNSTABLE representative for Rs.50000 — run1=TRD-3(...) run2=TRD-1(...) same? false
Oct 30, 2026 7:09:02 AM com.bank.sort.StableSorter sortByAmountThenSeq
INFO: Stable sort by (amount, trade_seq) — deterministic order on ties
INFO: STABLE representative for Rs.50000 — run1=TRD-1(...seq=1) run2=TRD-1(...seq=1) same? true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark's sort and orderBy are not stable, meaning they do not guarantee that rows with equal sort keys keep their original relative order. The reason is distribution: a DataFrame is split into partitions across executors, Spark range-shuffles the data so equal keys land together, and then sorts each partition in parallel before merging. The rows with equal keys can come from several source partitions and be interleaved in an order that depends on partitioning and task scheduling, so two runs of the same job can place tied rows differently. This is different from a single-machine sort where stability can be guaranteed on one list.

The practical consequence is that any logic relying on the order of equal keys is non-deterministic, such as picking the first row per group as a representative, generating sequence numbers, or producing output that an auditor expects to look identical every time. The fix is to make the full sort key unique by adding a tie-breaker. If the data has a natural monotonic column like a source sequence number or a trade timestamp with a counter, you sort by amount and then that column. If there is no such column, Spark provides monotonically increasing id, which you add as a column and include in the order by, giving you repeatable ordering, and the same principle applies to window functions, where you must put a unique column in the order by clause to get reproducible row numbers.

At the National Bank of India I ran into this when a settlement report sorted trades by amount and a downstream step chose the first trade in each amount bucket as the reconciliation representative. With identical data the chosen trade changed between runs, which alarmed the audit team. The cause was exactly the unstable sort on equal amounts. I fixed it by ordering on amount and then the trade's natural sequence number, which made every row's sort key unique and the output fully reproducible, and where a natural column did not exist I captured a monotonically increasing id right after reading the data. The rule I follow now is to never depend on the order of equal keys from a bare sort, and to always add a deterministic tie-breaker whenever correctness, reproducibility, or auditability depends on the ordering.
